title: Light as Photons: PAR and ePAR
objective: Distinguish photon-based plant-light measurements from human-vision and energy measurements, and state the wavelength band used for every value.

terms.definition: Discrete packet of electromagnetic radiation; photon energy increases as wavelength becomes shorter.
Photosynthetically active radiation conventionally counted from 400 through 700 nm.
Proposed extended photosynthetic range from 400 through 750 nm that includes far-red photons.
Photon flux density within a stated wavelength band, expressed as micromoles of photons per square metre per second.

coreScience: Plants intercept photons, not lumens. Lumens weight radiation according to human visual sensitivity, while photosynthetic photon measurements count photons within a declared waveband. Irradiance in watts per square metre describes radiant energy, not photon number; the same radiant energy contains more red photons than blue photons because longer-wavelength photons carry less energy individually.

PAR is a measurement convention, not a substance emitted by a lamp. A conventional quantum sensor integrates photons from 400 to 700 nm and reports PPFD. Research showing that far-red photons can contribute to photosynthesis when combined with shorter wavelengths led to the proposed 400-750 nm ePAR range. PAR-PPFD and ePAR-ePPFD values are therefore not interchangeable.

A spectral photon distribution is the most complete description because it shows photon delivery by wavelength. A single integrated number cannot reveal blue fraction, green fraction, red peaks, far-red content, ultraviolet output, or sensor mismatch. Every record must pair the numerical value with the band, sensor model, calibration basis, location, and operating state.
cultivationRelevance: Fixture comparisons fail when one map uses 400-700 nm and another uses 400-750 nm. Labeling the band prevents an apparent intensity gain from being mistaken for a real change in conventional PPFD.
Spectrum decisions should connect photon distribution to canopy response, morphology, photoreceptor signaling, safety, energy, and measured crop outcomes rather than to color names alone.

measureAndRecord.requirement: 400-700 nm PAR, 400-750 nm ePAR, or another explicitly defined range.
Manufacturer, model, serial number, sensor type, cosine response, calibration date, and correction factor if used.
Fixture or sunlight condition, dimming level, spectrum channel settings, warm-up time, and operating voltage.
Sensor height, orientation, distance from fixture, canopy state, walls or curtains, and grid location.
PPFD or ePPFD in micromoles per square metre per second, with timestamp and uncertainty notes.

misconceptions: PAR is light plants use equally: PAR defines a counting band; absorption, photosynthetic efficiency, signaling, and penetration still vary with wavelength and context.
Lux converts reliably to PPFD: Conversion depends strongly on the source spectrum and meter response; a generic factor can be seriously wrong.
ePAR replaces every PAR record: The bands answer different questions and must remain labeled for comparability with research, specifications, and historical data.
evidenceLimits: The 400-750 nm ePAR proposal is supported by plant research but conventional 400-700 nm PPFD remains deeply embedded in instruments, standards, research, and crop records. Cannabis-specific ePAR response data are still limited.

overview: Photon measurements count photons in a specified wavelength interval. Conventional PAR uses 400–700 nm and ePAR uses 400–750 nm; the same light source can produce different integrated values depending on the band. Neither is equivalent to lux or radiant watts.

mechanisms.heading: Photon count versus energy
mechanisms.body: The energy of one photon is E = hc/λ, so at equal radiant power longer-wavelength light contains more photons. PPFD integrates photon flux over the stated band, rather than weighting wavelengths for human vision.

mechanisms.heading: PAR and ePAR
mechanisms.body: Conventional PPFD integrates 400–700 nm; ePPFD integrates 400–750 nm and includes 700–750 nm far-red. Far-red can contribute to photosynthesis in combination with shorter wavelengths; the extra band also influences phytochrome signaling and morphology.

mechanisms.heading: Instrument response
mechanisms.body: Sensor spectral response, cosine response, calibration spectrum, geometry and channel settings can bias readings. A 400–700 nm meter cannot recover 700–750 nm photons from its integrated PPFD reading.

practicalInterpretation: Write the wavelength interval beside every photon flux value and map; never compare ePPFD against PPFD without accounting for the extra band.
Measure the same canopy grid at a recorded fixture height, dimmer setting, warm-up state and sensor orientation; keep instrument calibration details.
Use a spectroradiometer or suitable measured spectral data when a question depends on wavelength composition rather than integrated photon count.
limitationsAndUncertainty: A band-integrated count is not a universal photosynthetic efficiency or crop-yield prediction. Spectrum, plant acclimation and environment affect outcomes.
The diagram shows wavelength boundaries, not an actual lamp spectrum, relative photon quantities or an experimentally derived plant response curve.
Some instruments label ePAR differently; verify the manufacturer’s stated bandpass and calibration rather than relying on the label alone.
